scenes.title: Scaling
scenes.subtitle: More pods when the load climbs

lines.text: Nine o'clock on Monday, and the whole company opens go slash standup at once.
Two pods have been plenty so far. Today we let Kubernetes add more when the load climbs, and take them away again after.

scenes.title: Bigger pods, or more of them

boxes.label: limited by the size of one node
spreads the load over every node
more golinks pods, more queries for the one database

lines.text: There are two ways to handle more load. One is a bigger pod: more CPU for the same pod.
That only goes as far as the biggest node, and changing it means restarting the pod.
The other is more pods, sharing the work. That's horizontal scaling, and it's what we'll set up.
It works for golinks because the pods keep nothing of their own. Every link lives in Postgres, so any pod can answer any request.
lines.say: It works for go links because the pods keep nothing of their own. Every link lives in Postgres, so any pod can answer any request.

lines.text: Postgres is different. It's one pod that holds the data, and a second copy would need replication, which Episode 4 left out of scope.
So more golinks pods means more queries for that one database. Scaling moves the pressure along; it doesn't make it disappear.
lines.say: So more go links pods means more queries for that one database. Scaling moves the pressure along; it doesn't make it disappear.

lines.text: To scale on load, something has to measure it. k3s ships metrics-server, which asks every kubelet how much CPU and memory each pod is using.
kubectl top shows what it collects. CPU is in millicores: a thousand make one core.
So this pod is using 3 millicores. It asked for 100, a tenth of a core, back in Episode 2. That's 3 percent of its request.
lines.say: So this pod is using three millicores. It asked for a hundred, a tenth of a core, back in Episode 2. That's three percent of its request.

lines.text: That percentage, use against request, is exactly what the autoscaler watches. It's why every pod that scales needs an honest CPU request.
Here's the autoscaler, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, or HPA for short. Version 2 of the autoscaling API.
It points at the golinks Deployment. It never touches pods itself; it only changes the Deployment's replica count.
lines.say: It points at the go links Deployment. It never touches pods itself; it only changes the Deployment's replica count.

lines.text: Never fewer than two pods, so one can fail without an outage. Never more than six.
And the goal: average CPU use across the pods, at 70 percent of what they request.
Why not 100? A new pod takes a little while to start and turn ready, and the others carry the extra load until it does.
Last, how fast it scales back down. It waits for five minutes of lower load before it removes any pods.

boxes.label: within 10% of the target: no change

lines.text: The HPA is one more controller, like the ones in Episode 0. Every 15 seconds it reads the numbers, and sets the replica count.
The math is simple. Take the number of pods, multiply by how far use is over or under the target, and round up.
Two pods at 182 percent of their request: 182 over 70 is 2.6, times two pods, 5.2. Round up to six.
lines.say: Two pods at a hundred and eighty two percent of their request: a hundred and eighty two over seventy is two point six, times two pods, five point two. Round up to six.

lines.text: If use is within 10 percent of the target, it leaves things alone, so small wobbles don't add and remove pods.
lines.say: If use is within ten percent of the target, it leaves things alone, so small wobbles don't add and remove pods.

lines.text: And the answer always stays between the minimum and the maximum.
One change to the Deployment. Since Episode 2 it said replicas: 2. Now the HPA owns that number, so we take it out.
Otherwise, every apply of this file would set the count back to two, even at the busiest moment.
That matters even more in Episode 13, when Argo CD applies the files for us, again and again.
One catch: the first apply without it drops the count to one, the default, until the HPA's next check puts it back to two.

steps.command: kubectl get hpa golinks -n golinks | cut -c 32-

lines.text: Apply the HPA first, so it's already in charge.
Then the Deployment, without its replica count.
cut trims off the name columns, so it fits. 3 percent of the target CPU, two pods, between two and six. Quiet, as expected.
lines.say: Cut trims off the name columns, so it fits. Three percent, against a target of seventy, two pods, between two and six. Quiet, as expected.

steps.command: kubectl get hpa golinks -n golinks -w | cut -c 32-

lines.text: Now, Monday morning. The load test goes to the standup link, from the laptop, through every hop of the last episode.
hey sends requests from 50 workers at once, for three minutes, and doesn't follow the redirects, so only our cluster feels it.
lines.say: The hey tool sends requests from fifty workers at once, for three minutes, and doesn't follow the redirects, so only our cluster feels it.

lines.text: And watch the HPA. The w flag prints a new line whenever it changes.
lines.say: And watch the HPA. The W flag prints a new line whenever it changes.

lines.text: Soon, CPU is at 182 percent of the request. That's allowed: there's no CPU limit, so a busy pod can use more than it asked for.
lines.say: Soon, CPU is at a hundred and eighty two percent of the request. That's allowed: there's no CPU limit, so a busy pod can use more than it asked for.

lines.text: On its next check, the HPA does the math from before, and asks for six pods. It can add that many in one go, and it does.
Once the new pods are ready and sharing the work, the average settles at 61 percent, under the target. Six it stays.
lines.say: Once the new pods are ready and sharing the work, the average settles at sixty one percent, under the target. Six it stays.

steps.command: kubectl get pods -n golinks -o wide | awk '{print $1,$2,$5,$7}' | column -t

lines.text: Here they are: four new pods, 50 seconds old, three on each agent.
lines.say: Here they are: four new pods, fifty seconds old, three on each agent.

lines.text: None went to the server. As in Episode 2, it has only 50 millicores left unrequested, and each pod asks for 100.
lines.say: None went to the server. As in Episode 2, it has only fifty millicores left unrequested, and each pod asks for a hundred.

lines.text: Each new pod got traffic only once its readiness probe passed, and Traefik saw it in the EndpointSlice. Nobody touched the Ingress or the Service.

steps.command: kubectl get hpa golinks -n golinks -w | cut -c 32-

lines.text: Three minutes later, hey is done: about 1,200 requests a second, every one a 302.
lines.say: Three minutes later, hey is done: about twelve hundred requests a second, every one a three oh two.

lines.text: Back to the HPA. The load is gone and CPU drops to 2 percent, but it keeps six pods.
lines.say: Back to the HPA. The load is gone and CPU drops to two percent, but it keeps six pods.

lines.text: That's the five minute wait from the manifest. Real load often comes in waves, and removing pods just before the next wave would be the worst timing.
Five minutes of quiet later, it goes straight back down to the minimum, two.

scenes.title: On-prem, the nodes are the ceiling

boxes.label: set maxReplicas to what the nodes can hold

lines.text: Six pods fit easily. But say we'd set the maximum to 60.
lines.say: Six pods fit easily. But say we'd set the maximum to sixty.

lines.text: The scheduler places pods by their requests, and sooner or later the requests fill both agents.
The next pods stay Pending. The scheduler's message says why: no node has enough CPU left to promise.
In the cloud, that's when a new machine would appear. On-prem, the servers you have are the servers you have, and the HPA can only use the room that's on them.
So set the maximum to what the nodes can really hold, with the other apps' requests counted, and leave space for a node to fail.

boxes.label: on-prem VMs: Cluster API, with a vSphere provider
fixed servers, like ours: nothing to add

lines.text: Clusters that can add machines do it with one more controller. A node autoscaler watches for pods stuck Pending because nothing has room.
When it sees them, it asks the infrastructure underneath for another machine.
The machine boots, joins the cluster as a node, and the scheduler puts the waiting pods on it.
It works the other way too. When a node sits mostly empty, the autoscaler moves its pods elsewhere and gives the machine back.
In the cloud, that's the Cluster Autoscaler, or Karpenter, asking the cloud for virtual machines.
On-prem, it only works if machines can be made on demand: with virtual machines, Cluster API and a vSphere provider can create new nodes.
lines.say: On-prem, it only works if machines can be made on demand: with virtual machines, Cluster A P I and a V sphere provider can create new nodes.

lines.text: With a fixed set of servers, like ours, there's nothing to add. Capacity is planned ahead, and the HPA works inside it.

scenes.title: Episode 12: Kustomize
scenes.subtitle: One app, a dev and a prod

lines.text: So that's scaling: honest requests, an HPA that adds pods when they're busy, and a ceiling set by the nodes.
Next time: the same app in dev and in prod, with small differences, like this HPA's minimum and maximum. That's Kustomize.
